nodes.label: Limits
nodes.overview: A limit is the value a function approaches as its input gets close to a point, whether or not the function is defined there. Limits are the foundation for both derivatives and integrals.
points: The left-hand and right-hand limits must agree for the limit to exist
Limits at infinity describe end behavior and horizontal asymptotes
Forms like 0/0 are indeterminate and need algebra or L'Hopital's rule

cards.q: What does it mean for the limit of f(x) as x approaches a to equal L?
cards.a: f(x) gets as close to L as you like when x is close enough to a, from both sides.

cards.q: When does a two-sided limit fail to exist?
cards.a: When the left and right limits differ, or the function blows up or oscillates near the point.

nodes.label: Derivatives
nodes.overview: The derivative measures how fast a function is changing at a single point. Geometrically it is the slope of the tangent line; physically it is an instantaneous rate such as velocity.
points: Defined as the limit of the difference quotient as h goes to 0
Power rule: the derivative of x^n is n*x^(n-1)
Product and quotient rules handle combined functions
Where the derivative is zero, the function may have a maximum or minimum

cards.q: What is the limit definition of the derivative?
cards.a: f'(x) is the limit as h goes to 0 of (f(x + h) - f(x)) / h.

cards.q: What is the derivative of x^n?
cards.a: n * x^(n-1), the power rule.

cards.q: What does the sign of f'(x) tell you?
cards.a: Positive means f is increasing there; negative means it is decreasing.

nodes.label: Chain Rule
nodes.overview: The chain rule differentiates a function inside another function: take the derivative of the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the derivative of the inside.
points: If y = f(g(x)), then y' = f'(g(x)) * g'(x)
Work from the outermost function inward
It is the reason implicit differentiation and related rates work

cards.q: State the chain rule for y = f(g(x)).
Differentiate sin(3x^2).

nodes.label: Related Rates
nodes.overview: Related rates problems connect how fast two or more quantities change over time. You write one equation linking the quantities, then differentiate both sides with respect to time.
points: Draw the situation and name every changing quantity
Differentiate with respect to t using the chain rule
Plug in the numbers only after differentiating

cards.q: What is the most common mistake in related rates?
cards.a: Substituting values before differentiating, which turns a changing quantity into a constant.

cards.q: A circle's radius grows at 2 cm/s. How fast is the area growing when r = 5 cm?
cards.a: dA/dt = 2*pi*r*dr/dt = 20*pi cm^2/s.

nodes.label: Optimization
nodes.overview: Optimization uses derivatives to find the largest or smallest value of a quantity under a constraint, like the least material for a given volume.
points: Write the quantity to optimize as a function of one variable
Critical points are where the derivative is zero or undefined
Check endpoints as well as critical points on a closed interval
The second derivative tells a maximum from a minimum

cards.q: What are the steps of an optimization problem?
cards.a: Write the objective, use the constraint to get one variable, differentiate, set to zero, then check which candidates are the max or min.

cards.q: How does the second derivative test work?
cards.a: At a critical point, f'' > 0 means a local minimum and f'' < 0 means a local maximum.

nodes.label: Integrals
nodes.overview: An integral adds up infinitely many thin slices. The definite integral gives the signed area under a curve; the indefinite integral is the family of antiderivatives.
points: A definite integral is the limit of Riemann sums
Area below the x-axis counts as negative
Indefinite integrals always carry a constant of integration, + C

cards.q: What does the definite integral of f from a to b represent?
cards.a: The signed area between the graph of f and the x-axis from a to b.

cards.q: Why does an indefinite integral need + C?
cards.a: Because any constant disappears when you differentiate, so every antiderivative differs by a constant.

nodes.label: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
nodes.overview: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus says differentiation and integration undo each other. It turns the hard problem of summing slices into the easier one of finding an antiderivative.
points: Part 1: the derivative of the integral from a to x of f(t) dt is f(x)
Part 2: the integral from a to b of f equals F(b) - F(a), where F' = f
It links the area problem to the tangent problem

cards.q: State Part 2 of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.
cards.a: If F is an antiderivative of f, the integral of f from a to b equals F(b) - F(a).

cards.q: What is the derivative of the integral from 0 to x of cos(t) dt?
cards.a: cos(x), by Part 1.

nodes.label: u-Substitution
nodes.overview: u-substitution is the chain rule run backwards. You pick an inside function u whose derivative also appears in the integrand, which turns the integral into a simpler one.
points: Choose u as the inside function
Replace dx using du = u'(x) dx
For definite integrals, change the limits to u-values

cards.q: How do you choose u in a u-substitution?
cards.a: Pick the inside function whose derivative, up to a constant, is also in the integrand.

cards.q: Integrate 2x * cos(x^2) dx.
cards.a: Let u = x^2, du = 2x dx. The result is sin(x^2) + C.

nodes.label: Partial Derivatives
nodes.overview: A partial derivative measures how a function of several variables changes when one input changes and the others are held fixed.
points: Treat every other variable as a constant
The gradient collects all the partial derivatives into a vector
The gradient points in the direction of steepest increase

cards.q: How do you take the partial derivative with respect to x?
cards.a: Differentiate with respect to x while treating all other variables as constants.

cards.q: What does the gradient of f tell you?
cards.a: The direction in which f increases fastest, and how steep that increase is.

nodes.label: Multiple Integrals
nodes.overview: Double and triple integrals add up a quantity over a region of the plane or of space, such as volume under a surface or the mass of an object with varying density.
points: Evaluate as iterated integrals, one variable at a time
The order of integration can often be swapped (Fubini's theorem)
Polar coordinates simplify circular regions: dA = r dr d(theta)

cards.q: What does a double integral of f over a region R compute?
cards.a: The volume under the surface z = f(x, y) above R, counted with sign.

cards.q: What is the area element in polar coordinates?
cards.a: dA = r dr d(theta).

nodes.label: Vectors
nodes.overview: Vectors have both size and direction. Most of mechanics is done by breaking vectors into components along chosen axes and working with each axis separately.
points: Components: Ax = A cos(theta), Ay = A sin(theta)
Add vectors by adding their components
The dot product gives a scalar; the cross product gives a perpendicular vector

cards.q: How do you add two vectors?
cards.a: Add their x-components and their y-components separately.

cards.q: What does the dot product of two perpendicular vectors equal?
cards.a: Zero.

nodes.label: Kinematics
nodes.overview: Kinematics describes motion without asking what causes it. Position, velocity and acceleration are linked by derivatives, and for constant acceleration by a small set of equations.
points: Velocity is the derivative of position; acceleration is the derivative of velocity
v = v0 + a*t

cards.q: Which kinematic equation does not involve time?
How are position, velocity and acceleration related?
cards.a: Velocity is the time derivative of position, and acceleration is the time derivative of velocity.

nodes.label: Projectile Motion
nodes.overview: A projectile moves under gravity alone. Its horizontal and vertical motions are independent: constant velocity sideways, constant acceleration downward.
points: Horizontal: ax = 0, so vx stays constant
Vertical: ay = -g, about 9.8 m/s^2 downward
On level ground, range is greatest at a 45 degree launch angle
The path is a parabola

cards.q: What is the horizontal acceleration of a projectile, ignoring air resistance?
cards.a: Zero. The horizontal velocity stays constant.

cards.q: At the top of its path, what are a projectile's velocity and acceleration?
cards.a: The vertical velocity is zero, the horizontal velocity is unchanged, and the acceleration is still g downward.

nodes.label: Newton's Laws
nodes.overview: Newton's three laws connect forces to motion. They are the core model for everything from blocks on ramps to aircraft in flight.
points: First law: with no net force, velocity does not change
Second law: net force equals mass times acceleration
Third law: forces come in equal and opposite pairs on different objects

cards.q: State Newton's second law.
cards.a: The net force on an object equals its mass times its acceleration: F = m*a.

cards.q: Why don't action-reaction pairs cancel?
cards.a: Because the two forces act on different objects.

nodes.label: Work & Energy
nodes.overview: Work is energy transferred by a force acting over a distance. Tracking energy instead of forces often makes a problem much shorter.
points: Work: W = F*d*cos(theta)
Kinetic energy: K = (1/2)*m*v^2
Work-energy theorem: net work equals the change in kinetic energy
Mechanical energy is conserved when only conservative forces do work

cards.q: State the work-energy theorem.
cards.a: The net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy.

cards.q: When is mechanical energy conserved?
cards.a: When only conservative forces, like gravity and ideal springs, do work.

nodes.label: Momentum & Collisions
nodes.overview: Momentum is mass times velocity. In a collision the total momentum of an isolated system stays the same, even when kinetic energy does not.
points: p = m*v, a vector
Impulse equals the change in momentum: F*dt = dp
Elastic collisions conserve kinetic energy; inelastic ones do not

cards.q: What is conserved in every collision of an isolated system?
cards.a: Total momentum.

cards.q: What separates an elastic from an inelastic collision?
cards.a: Kinetic energy is conserved in an elastic collision and partly lost in an inelastic one.

nodes.label: Rotational Motion
nodes.overview: Rotational motion mirrors linear motion: angle replaces position, angular velocity replaces velocity, and moment of inertia replaces mass.
points: Angular velocity omega = d(theta)/dt, and v = r*omega
Moment of inertia depends on how mass is spread around the axis
Rotational kinetic energy: K = (1/2)*I*omega^2

cards.q: What plays the role of mass in rotation?
cards.a: The moment of inertia, I.

cards.q: How is linear speed related to angular speed?
cards.a: v = r * omega, where r is the distance from the axis.

nodes.label: Torque
nodes.overview: Torque is the turning effect of a force. It depends on the size of the force, how far from the axis it acts, and the angle it makes.
points: tau = r*F*sin(theta)
Net torque equals moment of inertia times angular acceleration
An object in static equilibrium has zero net force and zero net torque

cards.q: What is the formula for torque?
cards.a: tau = r * F * sin(theta), with r the distance from the axis to where the force acts.

cards.q: What are the two conditions for static equilibrium?
cards.a: The net force is zero and the net torque is zero.

nodes.label: Simple Harmonic Motion
nodes.overview: Simple harmonic motion is the back-and-forth motion that happens when the restoring force is proportional to displacement, as with a spring or a small-angle pendulum.
points: Restoring force: F = -k*x
Spring period: T = 2*pi*sqrt(m/k)
Pendulum period: T = 2*pi*sqrt(L/g), independent of mass
Energy trades between kinetic and potential

cards.q: What sets the period of a simple pendulum?
cards.a: Its length and g: T = 2*pi*sqrt(L/g). Mass and small amplitudes do not matter.

cards.q: What defines simple harmonic motion?
cards.a: A restoring force proportional to displacement and pointing back toward equilibrium.

nodes.label: Gravitation & Orbits
nodes.overview: Newton's law of gravitation says every pair of masses attracts with a force that falls off with the square of the distance. It explains both falling objects and orbits.
points: For a circular orbit, gravity supplies the centripetal force
Orbital speed: v = sqrt(G*M / r)
Kepler's third law: T^2 is proportional to r^3

cards.q: How does gravitational force change if the distance doubles?
cards.a: It drops to one quarter, because force goes as 1/r^2.

cards.q: What keeps a satellite in a circular orbit?
cards.a: Gravity, acting as the centripetal force.

nodes.label: Engineering Design Process
nodes.overview: The engineering design process is a loop, not a straight line: define the problem, research, brainstorm, prototype, test, and improve until the design meets its requirements.
points: Start from the user's need and measurable requirements
Generate several concepts before choosing one
Test early, and expect to iterate

cards.q: Name the main stages of the engineering design process.
cards.a: Define the problem, research, generate concepts, select, prototype, test, and iterate.

cards.q: Why iterate instead of building the first idea?
cards.a: Testing reveals problems early, when they are cheap to fix.

nodes.label: Team Roles & Charters
nodes.overview: A team charter writes down roles, expectations and how the team makes decisions, before the pressure of deadlines arrives.
points: Typical roles: lead, recorder, scheduler, quality checker
Agree on how to communicate and how to handle missed work
Rotate roles so everyone practices each one

nodes.label: Units & Dimensional Analysis
nodes.overview: Dimensional analysis treats units as algebra. Carrying units through every step catches most calculation mistakes before they matter.
points: Every equation must be dimensionally consistent
Convert by multiplying by factors equal to one
Know both SI and US customary units

cards.q: What is the quickest check on a formula you are unsure of?
cards.a: Check that the units on both sides match.

cards.q: Convert 60 miles per hour to feet per second.
cards.a: 88 ft/s.

nodes.label: CAD Basics (SolidWorks)
nodes.overview: CAD builds 3D parts from 2D sketches. A good model is fully defined and captures design intent, so it updates cleanly when a dimension changes.
points: Sketch on a plane, then extrude, revolve or cut
Fully define sketches with dimensions and relations
Parts combine into assemblies using mates

cards.q: What does a fully defined sketch mean?
cards.a: Every size and position is fixed by a dimension or relation, so nothing can move by accident.

cards.q: What is design intent in CAD?
cards.a: Building the model so that it changes the way you want when a dimension is edited.

nodes.label: Free-Body Diagrams
nodes.overview: A free-body diagram isolates one object and shows every external force acting on it. It is the first step in almost any statics or dynamics problem.
points: Draw only forces acting ON the object
Include weight, normal force, friction, tension and applied loads
Choose axes that make the components simple

cards.q: What belongs on a free-body diagram?
cards.a: Only the external forces acting on the chosen object, drawn at their points of action.

cards.q: What is a common free-body diagram error?
cards.a: Including forces the object exerts on other things, or inventing a force of motion.

nodes.label: Lift, Drag & Airfoils
nodes.overview: A wing produces lift by turning the airflow downward, and pays for it in drag. Lift and drag both grow with air density, the square of speed, and wing area.
points: Lift: L = (1/2)*rho*v^2*S*CL
Drag: D = (1/2)*rho*v^2*S*CD
Lift coefficient rises with angle of attack until the wing stalls
In steady level flight, lift equals weight and thrust equals drag

cards.q: What happens to lift if airspeed doubles?
cards.a: It roughly quadruples, because lift goes with the square of speed.

cards.q: What is a stall?
cards.a: The loss of lift when the angle of attack is too high and the airflow separates from the wing.

nodes.label: Engineering Ethics
nodes.overview: Engineering ethics puts public safety, health and welfare first. Professional codes guide what to do when cost, schedule and safety pull in different directions.
points: The public's safety comes before the employer's interest
Only do work you are competent to do
Be honest about data, limits and risks

cards.q: What is the first duty in most engineering codes of ethics?
cards.a: To hold paramount the safety, health and welfare of the public.

cards.q: What should an engineer do when asked to sign off on work outside their expertise?
cards.a: Decline, or bring in someone qualified.

nodes.label: Technical Reports
nodes.overview: A technical report lets a busy reader find the result fast and check how you got it. Structure and clear figures matter as much as the content.
points: Typical order: summary, introduction, methods, results, discussion, conclusion
Put the main result in the summary
Every figure and table needs a number, a caption and a mention in the text

cards.q: What goes in an executive summary?
cards.a: The problem, what was done, the main results and the recommendation, short enough to stand alone.

cards.q: What must every figure in a report have?
cards.a: A number, a caption, and a reference to it in the text.

nodes.label: Design Review Presentation
nodes.overview: A design review presents the design to people outside the team so they can find problems while changes are still cheap.
points: State the requirements, then show how the design meets them
Show the evidence: calculations, tests and prototypes
Name the open risks and the next steps

cards.q: What is the purpose of a design review?
cards.a: To get outside eyes on the design and catch problems before more time and money are spent.

nodes.label: Rhetorical Analysis
nodes.overview: Rhetorical analysis looks at how a text persuades, not only at what it says: who is speaking, to whom, for what purpose, and with which appeals.
points: Ethos: the writer's credibility
Pathos: appeals to emotion
Logos: reasoning and evidence
Consider audience, purpose and context together

cards.q: What are the three classical rhetorical appeals?
cards.a: Ethos (credibility), pathos (emotion) and logos (logic).

cards.q: What does a rhetorical analysis evaluate?
cards.a: How effectively a text persuades its audience, not whether you agree with it.

nodes.label: Thesis Statements
nodes.overview: A thesis statement is the one-sentence claim the whole essay defends. A good one is specific, arguable, and narrow enough to prove in the space available.
points: Takes a position someone could disagree with
Previews the main reasons
Usually sits at the end of the introduction

cards.q: What makes a thesis arguable?
cards.a: A reasonable reader could disagree with it, so it needs evidence to defend.

cards.q: What is wrong with a thesis that states a fact?
cards.a: There is nothing to argue, so the essay has no purpose.

nodes.label: Evaluating Sources
nodes.overview: Evaluating sources means deciding how much to trust what you read. Check who wrote it, why, how current it is, and whether others confirm it.
points: Authority: who is the author and what are their credentials?
Purpose: to inform, to sell or to persuade?
Peer-reviewed research carries more weight than opinion pieces
Read laterally: see what other sources say about this one

cards.q: What is lateral reading?
cards.a: Leaving a source to check what other reliable sources say about it.

cards.q: Name four things to check when evaluating a source.
cards.a: Authority, accuracy, currency and purpose.

nodes.label: Annotated Bibliography
nodes.overview: An annotated bibliography lists each source in full citation form, followed by a short paragraph that summarizes it and judges how useful it is.
points: Citation first, in the required style
Summarize the argument in a few sentences
Evaluate credibility and explain how you will use it

cards.q: What are the three parts of an annotation?
cards.a: A summary of the source, an evaluation of it, and a note on how it fits your project.

nodes.label: Argumentative Essay
nodes.overview: An argumentative essay makes a claim and supports it with reasons and evidence, while fairly answering the strongest objections.
points: Claim, reasons, evidence
Address a counterargument and respond to it
Each paragraph should advance one reason

cards.q: Why include a counterargument?
cards.a: Answering the strongest objection shows fairness and makes your own claim more convincing.

cards.q: What is the difference between a reason and evidence?
cards.a: A reason explains why the claim is true; evidence is the data or source that backs the reason.

nodes.label: MLA Citations
nodes.overview: MLA style gives credit to sources with short in-text citations that point to full entries on a Works Cited page.
points: In-text: author's last name and page number
Works Cited entries are alphabetical with a hanging indent
Cite paraphrases as well as direct quotations

cards.q: What goes in a basic MLA in-text citation?
cards.a: The author's last name and the page number, in parentheses.

cards.q: Do you need to cite a paraphrase?
cards.a: Yes. Ideas taken from a source need a citation even in your own words.

nodes.label: Peer Review
nodes.overview: Peer review is giving and getting feedback on a draft. The most useful comments are specific, focused on the big issues first, and suggest a way forward.
points: Start with thesis and structure before sentence-level edits
Point to a specific place and explain the effect on you as a reader
As the writer, decide which feedback to act on

nodes.label: Research Paper
nodes.overview: A research paper answers a focused question by bringing sources into conversation with each other and with your own argument.
points: Narrow the topic to a question you can answer
Synthesize sources instead of summarizing them one by one
Your voice and claim should lead; sources support

cards.q: What is synthesis in a research paper?
cards.a: Combining several sources to make a point of your own, instead of summarizing each one separately.

cards.q: What makes a good research question?
cards.a: It is focused, open to debate, and answerable with the sources and time you have.

nodes.label: Variables & Types
nodes.overview: A variable is a name that points to a value. Every value has a type, which decides what you can do with it.
points: Common types: int, float, str, bool
Python works out the type from the value
Convert between types with int(), float() and str()

cards.q: What is the difference between 7 / 2 and 7 // 2 in Python?
cards.a: 7 / 2 is 3.5 (true division); 7 // 2 is 3 (floor division).

cards.q: What type does input() return?
cards.a: A string, so numbers have to be converted.

nodes.label: Conditionals & Loops
nodes.overview: Conditionals choose which code runs; loops repeat code. Together they let a program make decisions and handle any amount of data.
points: if / elif / else pick one branch
for loops run once per item; while loops run until a condition fails
break leaves a loop early; continue skips to the next pass

cards.q: When should you use a while loop instead of a for loop?
cards.a: When you do not know in advance how many times it has to repeat.

cards.q: What does range(5) produce?
cards.a: The numbers 0, 1, 2, 3, 4.

nodes.label: Functions
nodes.overview: A function packages a piece of work under a name so it can be reused and tested. Inputs come in as parameters and the result goes out with return.
points: Define with def name(parameters):
return sends a value back; without it the function returns None
Variables created inside a function are local to it

cards.q: What is the difference between print and return?
cards.a: print shows a value on screen; return hands it back to the code that called the function.

cards.q: What does a function return if it has no return statement?
cards.a: None.

nodes.label: Lists & Dictionaries
nodes.overview: Lists hold items in order; dictionaries map keys to values. Picking the right one makes code both shorter and faster.
points: Lists are indexed from 0 and can be sliced
Dictionaries look up values by key
Both are mutable: they can be changed in place

cards.q: How do you get the last item of a list called items?
cards.a: items[-1].

cards.q: When is a dictionary better than a list?
cards.a: When you need to look things up by a name or key instead of by position.

nodes.label: File I/O & CSV
nodes.overview: File I/O lets a program keep data between runs. CSV files store tables as plain text, one row per line, which makes them easy to share with spreadsheets.
points: Use with open(...) so the file closes on its own
Modes: 'r' to read, 'w' to overwrite, 'a' to append
The csv module handles commas and quotes for you

cards.q: Why open files with a with statement?
cards.a: The file is closed automatically, even if an error happens.

cards.q: What does opening a file in 'w' mode do to its old contents?
cards.a: It erases them.

nodes.label: Classes & Objects
nodes.overview: A class is a blueprint for objects that bundle data with the functions that work on it. Classes keep larger programs organized.
points: __init__ sets up a new object's attributes
self refers to the object the method was called on
Inheritance lets one class build on another

cards.q: What is self in a method?
cards.a: The specific object the method is being called on.

cards.q: What is the job of __init__?
cards.a: To set the starting attributes when a new object is created.

nodes.label: NumPy Arrays
nodes.overview: NumPy arrays store numbers in a compact grid and apply operations to every element at once, which is far faster than looping in plain Python.
points: Arithmetic on arrays is element by element
Arrays have a fixed type and a shape
Use slicing and boolean masks to pick out data

cards.q: What is vectorization?
cards.a: Applying an operation to a whole array at once instead of looping over its elements.

cards.q: What does a.shape tell you?
cards.a: The size of the array along each dimension.

nodes.label: Plotting with Matplotlib
nodes.overview: Matplotlib turns arrays into charts. A clear plot has labeled axes, units, a title and a legend when there is more than one line.
points: plt.plot(x, y) for lines; plt.scatter for points
Always label axes and include units
plt.savefig writes the figure to a file

cards.q: What three things should every plot have?
cards.a: Labeled axes with units, a title, and a legend if there is more than one series.

cards.q: Which call draws a basic line chart?
cards.a: plt.plot(x, y), followed by plt.show().

nodes.label: pandas DataFrames
nodes.overview: A pandas DataFrame is a table with named columns. It makes loading, filtering, grouping and summarizing real data a few lines of code.
points: pd.read_csv loads a file into a DataFrame
Select a column with df['name']; filter rows with a condition
groupby splits the data, applies a function and combines the results

cards.q: How do you load a CSV file into pandas?
cards.a: pd.read_csv('file.csv').

cards.q: What does df.groupby('week')['sleep'].mean() do?
cards.a: It gives the average of the sleep column for each week.

nodes.label: Metronome Design Brief
nodes.overview: The design brief sets out what the metronome has to do, who it is for, and the limits on size, cost and time. Every later decision is checked against it.
points: Problem statement and target user
Requirements that can be measured, such as the tempo range
Constraints: budget, materials, deadline

cards.q: What is a design brief for?
cards.a: To pin down the problem, the user, the requirements and the constraints before designing anything.

nodes.label: Concept Sketches
nodes.overview: Concept sketches explore many possible forms quickly and cheaply. Quantity matters more than polish at this stage.
points: Sketch several different directions, not variations of one
Annotate with notes about function and materials
Pick a direction by comparing against the brief

nodes.label: Pendulum Mechanism
nodes.overview: A mechanical metronome keeps time with an inverted pendulum: a rod with a sliding weight above the pivot and a fixed weight below. Moving the top weight up slows the beat.
points: Sliding the weight away from the pivot lengthens the period
An escapement gives a small push each swing to replace lost energy
The click comes from the escapement, once per beat

cards.q: How does moving the sliding weight up change the tempo?
cards.a: It slows it down, because the pendulum's period gets longer.

cards.q: What does the escapement do?
cards.a: It feeds a little energy from the spring into each swing and makes the click.

nodes.label: Tempo Calibration (BPM)
nodes.overview: Tempo is measured in beats per minute. Calibrating the metronome means marking where the weight has to sit for each tempo and checking it against a reference.
points: Period in seconds = 60 / BPM
Typical range is about 40 to 208 BPM
Check against a timer or tuner app over many beats

cards.q: What is the time between beats at 120 BPM?
cards.a: 0.5 seconds.

cards.q: Why time many beats instead of one?
cards.a: Averaging over many beats makes the timing error much smaller.

nodes.label: Metronome CAD Model
nodes.overview: The CAD model defines every part of the metronome and how the parts fit together, so problems show up on screen instead of in the workshop.
points: Model each part, then build the assembly
Check clearances and the pendulum's range of motion
Drawings come from the model, with dimensions

cards.q: Why model the full assembly and not only the parts?
cards.a: To check that parts fit and move without colliding before anything is made.

nodes.label: 3D-Printed Prototype
nodes.overview: A 3D-printed prototype turns the model into something you can hold and test. The first print is for learning, not for looks.
points: Print orientation affects strength and surface finish
Leave clearance between moving parts
Write down what failed and feed it back into the model

cards.q: Why does print orientation matter?
cards.a: Printed parts are weakest between layers, and orientation also changes surface quality and the need for supports.

cards.q: What is the point of a first prototype?
cards.a: To find out what does not work while it is still cheap to change.

nodes.label: Portfolio Layout
nodes.overview: The portfolio tells the story of the project from problem to result. It shows the thinking and the iterations, not only the finished object.
points: Lead with the problem and the final result
Show process: sketches, models, failed prints, fixes
Keep the layout consistent and the captions short

cards.q: What should a design portfolio page show besides the final product?
cards.a: The process: the problem, the options considered, the testing and what changed as a result.

nodes.label: Product Renders
nodes.overview: Product renders are realistic images made from the CAD model. Lighting, materials and camera angle do most of the work.
points: Assign realistic materials and finishes
Use soft lighting and a simple background
Include one hero shot and a few detail views

nodes.label: Testosterone
nodes.overview: Testosterone is the main androgen. It supports muscle and bone, red blood cell production, libido, mood and energy. Levels follow a daily rhythm and are shaped by sleep, body composition, training and overall health.
points: Made mostly in the testes, under the control of signals from the brain
Highest in the morning, lower in the evening
Most of it travels bound to proteins; only a small share is free
Sleep loss, excess body fat and chronic stress are all linked to lower levels

cards.q: Where is most testosterone made, and what tells the body to make it?
cards.a: In the testes, in response to LH released by the pituitary gland.

cards.q: Why is the time of day important when testing testosterone?
cards.a: Levels peak in the morning, so tests are usually drawn early for a consistent comparison.

cards.q: Name three lifestyle factors linked to lower testosterone.
cards.a: Poor sleep, excess body fat and chronic stress.

nodes.label: Cortisol
nodes.overview: Cortisol is the body's main stress hormone. It follows a strong daily rhythm, helps mobilize energy and regulates inflammation. Short spikes are normal; staying high for long periods is the concern.
points: Peaks shortly after waking and falls through the day
Released through the HPA axis (hypothalamus, pituitary, adrenals)
Raised by stress, sleep loss and very hard training

cards.q: When is cortisol normally at its highest?
cards.a: In the first hour or so after waking.

cards.q: Which axis controls cortisol release?
cards.a: The HPA axis: hypothalamus, pituitary and adrenal glands.

nodes.label: Thyroid (T3 / T4)
nodes.overview: Thyroid hormones set the pace of metabolism in almost every tissue. The gland makes mostly T4, which the body converts into the more active T3.
points: T4 is the storage form; T3 is the active form
TSH from the pituitary tells the thyroid how much to make
Iodine and selenium are needed to make and convert thyroid hormone

cards.q: What is the difference between T4 and T3?
cards.a: T4 is the main hormone released by the thyroid; T3 is the more active form made from it.

cards.q: Which hormone signals the thyroid to produce more?
cards.a: TSH, from the pituitary gland.

nodes.label: Insulin Sensitivity
nodes.overview: Insulin moves glucose out of the blood and into cells. Insulin sensitivity describes how well cells respond: the better the response, the less insulin is needed for the same job.
points: Released by the pancreas after meals
Muscle is the largest sink for glucose
Activity, muscle mass and sleep improve sensitivity; excess body fat lowers it

cards.q: What does insulin sensitivity mean?
cards.a: How strongly cells respond to insulin. Higher sensitivity means less insulin is needed to clear glucose.

cards.q: Which tissue takes up most glucose after a meal?
cards.a: Skeletal muscle.

nodes.label: Estradiol
nodes.overview: Estradiol is the main estrogen. Men need it too, in smaller amounts, for bone health, libido and brain function. It is made from testosterone by the enzyme aromatase.
points: Produced from testosterone by aromatase
Aromatase is found in fat tissue, among other places
Both too little and too much cause problems

cards.q: How is estradiol made in men?
cards.a: The enzyme aromatase converts some testosterone into estradiol.

cards.q: Why is estradiol not simply a 'bad' hormone for men?
cards.a: It supports bone density, libido and brain function, so very low levels are also a problem.

nodes.label: SHBG
nodes.overview: Sex hormone-binding globulin is a protein made by the liver that carries testosterone and estradiol in the blood. Hormone bound to SHBG is not available to tissues.
points: Higher SHBG means less free testosterone for the same total
Tends to rise with age
Tends to be lower with insulin resistance and higher body fat

cards.q: What does SHBG do?
cards.a: It binds sex hormones in the blood, which keeps that portion from acting on tissues.

cards.q: Why can two people with the same total testosterone feel different?
cards.a: Their SHBG levels can differ, so the free, active share is not the same.

nodes.label: HPG Axis
nodes.overview: The HPG axis is the control loop for sex hormones. The hypothalamus releases GnRH, the pituitary answers with LH and FSH, and the gonads respond by making testosterone and sperm.
points: GnRH is released in pulses
LH drives testosterone production; FSH supports sperm production
Testosterone and estradiol feed back to turn the signal down

cards.q: What are the three levels of the HPG axis?
cards.a: Hypothalamus (GnRH), pituitary (LH and FSH), and gonads (testosterone).

cards.q: What is negative feedback in the HPG axis?
cards.a: Rising testosterone and estradiol signal the brain to release less GnRH and LH.

nodes.label: Growth Hormone
nodes.overview: Growth hormone supports tissue repair, growth and fat metabolism. Most of it is released in pulses, with the largest pulse early in the night during deep sleep.
points: Released by the pituitary in pulses
The biggest pulse comes with the first block of deep sleep
Many of its effects work through IGF-1, made in the liver

cards.q: When is the largest daily pulse of growth hormone released?
cards.a: Early in the night, during deep (slow-wave) sleep.

cards.q: Which hormone carries out many of growth hormone's effects?
cards.a: IGF-1, produced mainly by the liver.

nodes.label: Circadian Rhythm
nodes.overview: The circadian rhythm is the body's roughly 24-hour clock. It times sleep, body temperature and hormone release, and it is set mainly by light reaching the eyes.
points: The master clock sits in the brain's suprachiasmatic nucleus
Morning light moves the clock earlier; evening light moves it later
Melatonin rises in the evening as darkness falls

cards.q: What is the strongest signal for setting the body clock?
cards.a: Light, especially bright light in the morning.

cards.q: What does melatonin signal?
cards.a: That it is biological night; it rises in the evening in dim light.

nodes.label: Deep Sleep
nodes.overview: Deep sleep, also called slow-wave sleep, is the most physically restorative stage. Growth hormone is released, tissue is repaired, and the brain clears waste products.
points: Concentrated in the first half of the night
Hardest stage to wake from
Reduced by alcohol, late caffeine and a warm bedroom

cards.q: In which part of the night does most deep sleep occur?
cards.a: The first half.

cards.q: Why does deep sleep matter for recovery?
cards.a: It is when the largest growth hormone pulse occurs and when much physical repair takes place.

nodes.label: REM Sleep
nodes.overview: REM sleep is the stage with vivid dreaming. The brain is active while the body is still, and it is tied to memory, learning and emotional processing.
points: Concentrated in the second half of the night
Cutting sleep short removes mostly REM
Alcohol suppresses REM early in the night

cards.q: Which stage do you lose most of by waking two hours early?
cards.a: REM sleep, because it is concentrated late in the night.

cards.q: What is REM sleep linked to?
cards.a: Memory consolidation, learning and emotional regulation.

nodes.label: Consistent Wake Time
nodes.overview: Waking at the same time every day anchors the body clock. A stable wake time tends to make it easier to fall asleep at night and to wake without an alarm.
points: Wake time is easier to control than bedtime
Large weekend shifts act like jet lag
Light soon after waking strengthens the anchor

cards.q: Why anchor wake time instead of bedtime?
cards.a: You can control when you get up, and a steady wake time pulls the rest of the rhythm into line.

cards.q: What is social jet lag?
cards.a: The mismatch created by sleeping and waking much later on weekends than on weekdays.

nodes.label: Cool, Dark Bedroom
nodes.overview: The body cools slightly to fall asleep and stay asleep, and light at night signals daytime to the brain. A cool, dark, quiet room removes two common obstacles.
points: Core body temperature drops at sleep onset
Even dim light at night can reduce melatonin
Blackout curtains or an eye mask are simple fixes

cards.q: Why does a cooler room help sleep?
cards.a: Falling asleep goes with a drop in core body temperature, and a cool room makes that easier.

cards.q: How does light at night interfere with sleep?
cards.a: It suppresses melatonin and signals the body clock that it is still daytime.

nodes.label: Caffeine Cutoff
nodes.overview: Caffeine blocks adenosine, the chemical that builds up sleep pressure during the day. It lingers for hours, so an afternoon coffee can still be active at bedtime.
points: Half-life is roughly 5 to 6 hours, with wide variation between people
Can reduce deep sleep even if you fall asleep fine
A common rule is to stop 8 or more hours before bed

cards.q: How does caffeine keep you awake?
cards.a: It blocks adenosine receptors, masking the build-up of sleep pressure.

cards.q: Why can late caffeine hurt sleep even if you fall asleep normally?
cards.a: It can still be in your system and reduce the amount of deep sleep.

nodes.label: Sleep Tracking
nodes.overview: Sleep tracking turns nights into numbers you can compare. Wearables are good at total sleep time and timing, and much rougher at telling sleep stages apart.
points: Useful measures: duration, consistency, time to fall asleep
Stage estimates from wearables are approximate
Look at trends over weeks, not single nights

cards.q: What are consumer sleep trackers most reliable for?
cards.a: Total sleep time and sleep timing, more than exact sleep stages.

cards.q: Why look at weekly trends?
cards.a: Single nights vary a lot; trends show whether a change is real.

nodes.label: Resistance Training
nodes.overview: Resistance training means working muscles against a load. It builds muscle and strength, supports bone density, and improves how the body handles glucose.
points: Mechanical tension is the main driver of muscle growth
Most major muscle groups respond well to training about twice a week
Sets taken close to failure count the most

cards.q: What is the main stimulus for muscle growth?
cards.a: Mechanical tension from challenging sets taken close to failure.

cards.q: Name two benefits of resistance training beyond muscle size.
cards.a: Better bone density and better insulin sensitivity.

nodes.label: Progressive Overload
nodes.overview: Progressive overload means asking a little more of the body over time. Without it, the body has no reason to keep adapting.
points: Add weight, reps or sets gradually
Track workouts so progress is visible
Progress in small steps to avoid stalling or injury

cards.q: What is progressive overload?
cards.a: Gradually increasing the demand on the body, through load, reps or volume, so it keeps adapting.

cards.q: Why keep a training log?
cards.a: So you know what you did last time and can do slightly more.

nodes.label: Compound Lifts
nodes.overview: Compound lifts move more than one joint and work several muscle groups at once. They let you train a lot of muscle with heavy loads in little time.
points: Examples: squat, deadlift, bench press, overhead press, row, pull-up
Technique comes before load
Isolation exercises fill the gaps afterwards

cards.q: What makes a lift a compound lift?
cards.a: It involves movement at more than one joint and uses several muscle groups.

cards.q: Give three examples of compound lifts.
cards.a: Squat, deadlift and bench press.

nodes.label: Zone 2 Cardio
nodes.overview: Zone 2 is steady, easy aerobic work at a pace where you can still hold a conversation. It builds the aerobic base and the capacity of mitochondria to burn fat.
points: Roughly 60 to 70 percent of maximum heart rate
You should be able to speak in full sentences
Low stress, so it is easy to recover from

cards.q: How can you tell you are in zone 2 without a heart rate monitor?
cards.a: You can hold a conversation in full sentences, but would rather not sing.

cards.q: What does zone 2 training develop?
cards.a: Aerobic base and mitochondrial capacity.

nodes.label: Recovery & Deloads
nodes.overview: Training provides the signal; adaptation happens during recovery. Sleep, food and planned easier weeks are part of the program, not time off from it.
points: Sleep is the most important recovery tool
A deload week cuts volume or intensity on purpose
Soreness alone is a poor guide to recovery

cards.q: What is a deload?
cards.a: A planned period of lighter training that lets fatigue clear so progress can continue.

cards.q: When does the body actually get stronger?
cards.a: During recovery after training, not during the session itself.

nodes.label: Sprints & HIIT
nodes.overview: High-intensity intervals alternate short, very hard efforts with rest. They raise top-end fitness quickly, at the price of more fatigue than easy cardio.
points: Efforts of seconds to a few minutes, near maximum
Improves VO2 max in little total time
One or two sessions a week is plenty for most people

cards.q: What is the trade-off of high-intensity intervals?
cards.a: Large fitness benefits in little time, but more fatigue and a higher recovery cost.

cards.q: What does HIIT improve most?
cards.a: VO2 max, the upper limit of aerobic fitness.

nodes.label: Overtraining
nodes.overview: Overtraining is what happens when training load stays ahead of recovery for too long. Performance drops, and sleep, mood and hormones can all suffer.
points: Warning signs: falling performance, poor sleep, low mood, constant fatigue
Resting heart rate may rise
The fix is rest and more food, not more effort

cards.q: Name three warning signs of overtraining.
cards.a: Declining performance, disturbed sleep and persistent fatigue or low mood.

cards.q: What is the remedy for overtraining?
cards.a: Reducing training load and prioritizing sleep and nutrition until performance returns.

nodes.label: Protein Intake
nodes.overview: Protein supplies the amino acids used to build and repair muscle. Enough protein, spread through the day, supports training and helps you stay full.
points: A common target for people who train is about 1.6 to 2.2 g per kg of body weight per day
Spread across meals instead of one large serving
Complete sources contain all essential amino acids

cards.q: Why does protein matter for someone who lifts?
cards.a: It provides the amino acids needed to repair and build muscle after training.

cards.q: What is a complete protein?
cards.a: A source that contains all nine essential amino acids.

nodes.label: Dietary Fats & Cholesterol
nodes.overview: Dietary fat is a building material as well as a fuel. Cholesterol is the starting molecule for steroid hormones, and very low-fat diets have been linked to lower testosterone.
points: Steroid hormones, including testosterone, are made from cholesterol
Types: saturated, monounsaturated, polyunsaturated
Omega-3 fats come mainly from oily fish

cards.q: What molecule are steroid hormones made from?
cards.a: Cholesterol.

cards.q: Name the three main types of dietary fat.
cards.a: Saturated, monounsaturated and polyunsaturated.

nodes.label: Zinc & Magnesium
nodes.overview: Zinc and magnesium are minerals involved in hundreds of enzyme reactions, including hormone production, muscle function and sleep. Low intake is fairly common.
points: Zinc sources: red meat, shellfish, seeds
Magnesium sources: leafy greens, nuts, legumes
Correcting a deficiency helps; taking more than you need does not add benefit

cards.q: Name two food sources of zinc.
cards.a: Red meat and shellfish (oysters are especially rich).

cards.q: Does extra zinc raise testosterone in someone who is not deficient?
cards.a: Generally not. The benefit seen in studies comes from correcting a deficiency.

nodes.label: Vitamin D
nodes.overview: Vitamin D acts more like a hormone than a vitamin. The skin makes it from sunlight, and it supports bone, immune function and muscle. Low levels are common, especially in winter.
points: Made in the skin from UVB sunlight
Food sources are limited: oily fish, egg yolks, fortified foods
Status is checked with a blood test

cards.q: How does the body get most of its vitamin D?
cards.a: The skin makes it when exposed to UVB light from the sun.

cards.q: Why are low vitamin D levels common in winter?
cards.a: There is less sun and less skin exposed, so the skin makes much less.

nodes.label: Energy Balance
nodes.overview: Energy balance is calories in against calories out. Body weight follows it over time, and hormones respond to it: long, steep deficits tend to lower testosterone and thyroid output.
points: A surplus adds weight; a deficit removes it
Large, long deficits lower testosterone and thyroid hormones
Slower changes are easier on hormones and on muscle

cards.q: What happens to hormones in a long, aggressive calorie deficit?
cards.a: Testosterone and thyroid output tend to fall, and cortisol tends to rise.

cards.q: What is energy balance?
cards.a: The difference between calories eaten and calories burned.

nodes.label: Alcohol
nodes.overview: Alcohol is a sedative, not a sleep aid. It fragments sleep and suppresses REM, and heavy drinking is linked to lower testosterone.
points: Reduces REM sleep and causes more waking later in the night
Heavy intake is associated with lower testosterone
The effect scales with the amount and how close to bedtime

cards.q: How does alcohol affect sleep?
cards.a: It may help you fall asleep, but it fragments sleep and suppresses REM.

cards.q: What two things decide how much alcohol disrupts sleep?
cards.a: How much you drink and how close to bedtime.

nodes.label: Whole Foods
nodes.overview: Whole foods are foods close to how they were grown or raised. They bring more protein, fiber and micronutrients per calorie than ultra-processed foods, and are harder to overeat.
points: Built around meat, fish, eggs, fruit, vegetables, legumes and whole grains
Ultra-processed foods are easy to overeat
Less packaging can also mean less contact with plastics

cards.q: Why are whole foods harder to overeat?
cards.a: They are more filling per calorie because of their protein, fiber and water content.

cards.q: What is an ultra-processed food?
cards.a: An industrial product made mostly from refined ingredients and additives, with little intact whole food.

nodes.label: Endocrine Disruptors
nodes.overview: Endocrine disruptors are chemicals that interfere with the body's hormone system. They can mimic a hormone, block it, or change how it is made and broken down.
points: Examples: BPA, phthalates, PFAS, some pesticides
Exposure comes through food, water, air and skin
Effects can occur at low doses and depend on timing
Reducing exposure is easier than removing it

cards.q: What is an endocrine disruptor?
cards.a: A chemical that interferes with hormones by mimicking them, blocking them or altering how they are made or cleared.

cards.q: Name three groups of endocrine-disrupting chemicals.
cards.a: Bisphenols such as BPA, phthalates and PFAS.

cards.q: What are the main routes of exposure?
cards.a: Food and drink, air and dust, and contact with the skin.

nodes.label: Microplastics
nodes.overview: Microplastics are plastic particles smaller than 5 mm. They are now found in water, food, air and human tissue. Their health effects are an active area of research.
points: Shed from packaging, synthetic clothing and tires
Heating food in plastic increases shedding
Can carry additives such as phthalates

cards.q: What are microplastics?
cards.a: Plastic particles smaller than 5 millimeters.

cards.q: What everyday habit increases the release of plastic particles into food?
cards.a: Heating food or drinks in plastic containers.

nodes.label: BPA & Phthalates
nodes.overview: BPA and phthalates are two of the best-studied plastic chemicals. BPA can act like estrogen, and some phthalates are linked to lower testosterone in human studies.
points: BPA: can linings, some hard plastics, thermal receipts
Phthalates: soft plastics, fragrance, some personal care products
'BPA-free' products may use similar bisphenols

cards.q: Where is BPA commonly found?
cards.a: In the linings of food cans, some hard plastics and thermal paper receipts.

cards.q: What hormone effect are phthalates linked to?
cards.a: Lower testosterone, in a number of human studies.

cards.q: Why is 'BPA-free' not a guarantee?
cards.a: Replacement bisphenols such as BPS can behave in similar ways.

nodes.label: Blue Light at Night
nodes.overview: Light in the evening, especially the blue part of the spectrum, tells the body clock that it is still daytime. That delays melatonin and pushes sleep later.
points: Blue wavelengths suppress melatonin the most
Brightness and duration matter as much as color
Dimmer, warmer light in the last hours before bed helps

cards.q: How does evening light affect sleep?
cards.a: It suppresses melatonin and shifts the body clock later, making it harder to fall asleep.

cards.q: Which matters besides the color of evening light?
cards.a: How bright it is and how long you are exposed to it.

nodes.label: Morning Sunlight
nodes.overview: Bright light soon after waking is the strongest daily signal for the body clock. It helps set the timing of cortisol in the morning and melatonin at night.
points: Outdoor light is far brighter than indoor light, even on cloudy days
Early light moves the clock earlier
Pairs well with a consistent wake time

cards.q: Why is outdoor light better than indoor light in the morning?
cards.a: It is many times brighter, so it is a much stronger signal to the body clock.

cards.q: What does morning light do to the timing of sleep?
cards.a: It shifts the clock earlier, which makes it easier to fall asleep at night.

nodes.label: Water Filtration
nodes.overview: Tap water can carry small amounts of contaminants, including PFAS and microplastics. Filters differ a lot in what they remove.
points: Activated carbon reduces chlorine and some organic chemicals
Reverse osmosis removes the widest range, including most PFAS
Check a filter's certification for the specific contaminant

cards.q: Which filter type removes the widest range of contaminants?
cards.a: Reverse osmosis.

cards.q: How do you know what a filter actually removes?
cards.a: Check its independent certification for the specific contaminant.

nodes.label: PFAS
nodes.overview: PFAS are a large family of 'forever chemicals' used for nonstick, stain-resistant and water-repellent products. They break down very slowly and build up in the body.
points: Found in some nonstick cookware, food packaging and water supplies
Stay in the body for years
Linked in studies to thyroid and other hormone effects

cards.q: Why are PFAS called forever chemicals?
cards.a: They break down extremely slowly in the environment and stay in the body for years.

cards.q: Name two common sources of PFAS exposure.
cards.a: Contaminated drinking water and some nonstick or grease-resistant products.

nodes.label: Fragrance & Personal Care
nodes.overview: Fragrance in personal care products can contain phthalates, which help a scent last. Because the ingredient list often just says 'fragrance', they are easy to miss.
points: 'Fragrance' or 'parfum' can cover many undisclosed ingredients
Skin products are absorbed directly
Fragrance-free options avoid the question

cards.q: Why are phthalates used in fragranced products?
cards.a: They help the scent last longer.

cards.q: What is the simplest way to avoid phthalates from fragrance?
cards.a: Choose fragrance-free products.

nodes.label: Total Testosterone
nodes.overview: Total testosterone measures all testosterone in the blood, bound and free. It is the standard first test, and because levels vary through the day it is drawn in the morning.
points: Usually drawn in the morning, often fasted
Reported in ng/dL or nmol/L
One low result should be confirmed with a repeat test

cards.q: What does total testosterone measure?
cards.a: All testosterone in the blood: the part bound to proteins plus the free part.

cards.q: Why repeat a low testosterone result?
cards.a: Levels vary from day to day, so a diagnosis should not rest on a single test.

nodes.label: Free Testosterone
nodes.overview: Free testosterone is the small share not bound to proteins, and so the part that can act on tissues. It is often calculated from total testosterone, SHBG and albumin.
points: Roughly 1 to 3 percent of total testosterone
Useful when SHBG is unusually high or low
Calculated values are usually more reliable than direct assays

cards.q: What is free testosterone?
cards.a: The unbound fraction of testosterone that is available to tissues.

cards.q: When is free testosterone most informative?
cards.a: When SHBG is unusually high or low, so total testosterone is misleading.

nodes.label: Lipid Panel
nodes.overview: A lipid panel measures the fats carried in the blood. It is a core marker of cardiovascular risk and worth tracking alongside hormones.
points: Total cholesterol, LDL, HDL and triglycerides
ApoB counts the number of atherogenic particles
Triglycerides are sensitive to diet and are usually measured fasted

cards.q: What four values does a standard lipid panel report?
cards.a: Total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, HDL cholesterol and triglycerides.

cards.q: What does ApoB add to a lipid panel?
cards.a: A count of the particles that can drive plaque build-up, which predicts risk better than LDL cholesterol alone.

nodes.label: HbA1c & Fasting Glucose
nodes.overview: HbA1c reflects average blood glucose over about three months, while fasting glucose is a snapshot of one morning. Together they screen for insulin resistance and diabetes.
points: HbA1c is the share of hemoglobin with glucose attached
Fasting glucose is measured after at least 8 hours without food
Fasting insulin can reveal resistance before glucose rises

cards.q: What time span does HbA1c reflect?
cards.a: Roughly the past three months.

cards.q: Why measure fasting insulin as well as glucose?
cards.a: Insulin often rises years before glucose does, so it can show resistance earlier.

nodes.label: TSH
nodes.overview: TSH is the pituitary's signal to the thyroid, and the standard first screen of thyroid function. It moves in the opposite direction to thyroid hormone levels.
points: High TSH suggests an underactive thyroid
Low TSH suggests an overactive thyroid
Free T4 and free T3 are added when TSH is abnormal

cards.q: What does a high TSH usually indicate?
cards.a: An underactive thyroid: the pituitary is asking for more hormone.

cards.q: Which tests follow an abnormal TSH?
cards.a: Free T4 and free T3.

nodes.label: 25-OH Vitamin D
nodes.overview: 25-hydroxyvitamin D is the blood test for vitamin D status. It reflects both sun exposure and intake over the previous weeks.
points: Written as 25(OH)D
Reported in ng/mL or nmol/L
Tends to be lowest at the end of winter

cards.q: Which blood test measures vitamin D status?
cards.a: 25-hydroxyvitamin D, written 25(OH)D.

cards.q: When in the year is vitamin D usually lowest?
cards.a: At the end of winter.

nodes.label: Reference vs. Optimal Ranges
nodes.overview: A reference range covers the middle 95 percent of the people a lab has tested. It describes what is common, which is not always the same as what is best for health.
points: Reference ranges differ between labs
The tested population includes people who are not healthy
Trends in your own results over time matter more than one number

cards.q: What does a lab reference range represent?
cards.a: The range containing about 95 percent of results from the lab's reference population.

cards.q: Why is 'within range' not the same as optimal?
cards.a: The range describes what is common in the tested population, not what is associated with the best health.

nodes.label: Recruitment
nodes.overview: Recruitment is finding the first people to try Baseline. A small, engaged group that fits the target user is worth more than a large, passive one.
points: Define who the pilot is for before inviting anyone
Start with people who already care about the problem
Be clear about the time commitment

nodes.label: Onboarding Survey
nodes.overview: The onboarding survey captures each participant's starting point: habits, goals and context. It is the comparison point for everything measured later.
points: Ask only what will be used
Cover sleep, training, nutrition and environment
Explain how the data is stored and who can see it

cards.q: Why collect a survey before the pilot starts?
cards.a: It records the starting point, so later changes can be measured against it.

nodes.label: Baseline Labs
nodes.overview: Baseline labs are the blood tests taken before the protocol starts. Without them there is nothing to compare the end results to.
points: Same lab, same time of day, same fasting state as the follow-up
Morning draw for hormone tests
Record anything unusual about the day of the test

cards.q: Why must baseline and follow-up labs be drawn under the same conditions?
cards.a: Time of day, fasting and lab differences can change results as much as the protocol does.

cards.q: What is the purpose of baseline labs?
cards.a: To record each participant's starting values so changes can be measured.

nodes.label: Weekly Check-ins
nodes.overview: Weekly check-ins collect how participants are doing while the protocol runs: sleep, training, energy and what they found hard.
points: Keep them short enough to finish in two minutes
Same questions every week so answers can be compared
A missed check-in is itself a signal

cards.q: Why ask the same questions every week?
cards.a: So answers can be compared over time and trends are visible.

nodes.label: 8-Week Protocol
nodes.overview: The 8-week protocol is the plan participants follow: a small set of sleep, training, nutrition and environment habits, introduced in stages.
points: A few habits done consistently beat many done briefly
Introduce changes in stages, not all at once
Eight weeks is long enough for habits to settle and for labs to move

cards.q: Why introduce habits in stages?
cards.a: Changing everything at once is hard to stick to and hides which change made the difference.

cards.q: Why does the protocol run for eight weeks?
cards.a: It gives habits time to settle and is long enough for blood markers to change.

nodes.label: Retention
nodes.overview: Retention is the share of participants still active as the weeks go by. It shows whether the protocol fits into real life.
points: Track weekly check-in completion
Find out why people stop, not only how many
Early drop-off usually points at onboarding

nodes.label: Feedback Interviews
nodes.overview: Feedback interviews are conversations with participants at the end of the pilot. They explain the numbers: what worked, what did not, and why.
points: Ask open questions and listen more than you talk
Ask about specific moments, not general opinions
Look for patterns across interviews
